newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian Metals - Trade puzzled by Chinese zinc talk.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - Trade puzzled by Chinese zinc talk.

text.p: Far East base metal dealers were involved in a guessing game on Friday over how much Chinese zinc is bound for Singapore, with one saying up to 90,000 tonnes is on the way here while another put the figure as low as 5,000 tonnes.
Zinc dealers agree that the Chinese are delivering the metal to the London Metal Exchange (LME) warehouse in Singapore to cover their short positions.
But traders differed widely on the actual tonnages involved.
"I've been hearing news of 150,000 tonnes and 20,000 tonnes," said Vinod Kumar, director of metal company Donald Mcarthy.
"I believe the more likely figure is 80,000 to 90,000 tonnes," he said, adding the zinc will probably be delivered to the LME warehouse here in 1-1/2 to two months time.
But a Japanese zinc trader believed otherwise.
"I can tell you the quantity coming here is 5,000 tonnes and that about 10,000 tonnes remains off-warrant," he said. "Within a week, we should see some increase in the stock numbers here."
Another trader with a foreign metal dealing house said the current talk circulating in the market is that "the Chinese are shipping 20,000 tonnes. The rumour is they're moving 40,000."
The Chinese were caught on the wrong end of a speculative squeeze on the LME recently and have been forced to deliver material rather than take huge losses on the transaction.
"The question really is how much they're delivering," a trader said. "Frankly, nobody knows."
Kumar said the Chinese were busy melting thousands of tonnes of zinc and casting them into ingots for delivery.
"All the zinc laying in China is coming out now," he said. "A lot of zinc is going to come into Singapore."
Chinese officials were not immediately available for comment.

China's short position on the LME stood at around 200,000 to 250,000 tonnes, sold at around $1,100 a tonne earlier this year. Some of the positions have been covered after prices fell from a seven-year peak two weeks ago of more than $1,700 a tonne.
In other developments, aluminium premiums softened in Singapore after the backwardation on the LME flared overnight to as high as $20, having been level earlier this week.

Premiums for western 20-25 kg aluminium ingots eased to around $75-$85 a tonne from $75-$90 last week. Those for Indian and Russian 25-kg aluminium ingots were quoted by the trade at $60-$70 a tonne against $70-$75 last week.
Western ingot premiums hit a high of $95 about a month ago.
"With the backwardation, there's no reason to keep the material," a trader said. "The Koreans are selling it and putting it in warehouses in Japan."
Dealers said several thousand tonnes of aluminium were delivered by the Koreans into Japan.
The volume of aluminium in the LME's Yokohama warehouse reached 2,125 tonnes and 950 tonnes in Nagoya on Thursday.
Lead premiums, on the other hand, firmed in Singapore due to low stocks in the LME's Singapore warehouse, dealers said.
Premiums for 25-40 kg ingots climbed to $25-$40 a tonne from $20-$30 last week due mainly to tight supplies in the market.
The volume of lead in the Singapore warehouse reached 4,025 tonnes on Thursday against 6,375 tonnes in the middle of July.
"There's not a lot of tonnage left in Singapore," a dealer said. "That's why we could raise the premiums for lead."
"Lead is very firm," Kumar said.
